#4336. MIT scientists turn immune cells into cancer killers inside the body

MIT researchers have developed a new technique that allows them to transform immune cells into cancer fighters directly inside the body, potentially making advanced treatments for cancer and autoimmune diseases much easier to produce and administer.

The method focuses on natural killer (NK) cells, a type of immune cell that can be engineered to recognize and destroy harmful cells. These include cancerous T cells and T cells that mistakenly attack healthy tissue, contributing to conditions such as lymphoma and autoimmune hepatitis.

Rather than extracting immune cells from a patient and modifying them in a laboratory, the researchers use tiny particles made of fatty molecules to deliver genetic instructions directly to NK cells. These instructions, carried by messenger RNA, tell the cells to produce specialized proteins that help them identify and eliminate diseased T cells.

The resulting cells, known as CAR NK cells, could eventually be used against several different diseases. By carrying out the engineering process inside the body, the new approach could eliminate much of the time, expense, and complexity involved in manufacturing personalized immune cell therapies.

"The manufacturing challenges with CAR NK cells are significant. The idea here is you can deliver a nanoparticle that will modify your own NK cells with a CAR construct and teach them to attack tumor cells," says Daniel Anderson, a professor in MIT's Department of Chemical Engineering and a member of MIT's Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research and Institute for Medical Engineering and Science.

Anderson is the senior author of the research, published in Nature Biotechnology. The lead authors are MIT postdoctoral researcher Yuang Chen and graduate students Julia Monkovic and Haseeb Mughal. Robert Langer, MIT's David H. Koch Institute Professor, also contributed to the study.

Why Current Cancer Immunotherapies Are So Complex

Immune cell engineering has already transformed treatment options for certain cancers. During the past decade, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved seven cancer therapies that use genetically modified T cells, known as chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells.

These treatments work by equipping T cells with specially designed receptors that recognize particular markers, or antigens, on other cells. When an engineered T cell encounters its designated target, such as a protein associated with cancer, it becomes activated and attacks the cell carrying that marker.

CAR T cell therapies have been especially effective against blood cancers arising from B cells. These include certain forms of leukemia and lymphoma, as well as multiple myeloma.

However, preparing these treatments involves several complicated steps. Doctors first collect blood from the patient and send it to a specialized facility. There, technicians separate the T cells, genetically modify them to produce the desired receptors, and grow enough engineered cells for treatment. The finished cells must then be transported back to the hospital and infused into the patient.

Natural Killer Cells Offer a Different Way to Fight Cancer

Scientists have recently been exploring whether natural killer cells could be engineered in a similar way. One important advantage is their potential to treat cancers and autoimmune conditions involving abnormal T cells.

Trying to use CAR T cells against diseased T cells creates a major problem. Because both the engineered cells and their intended targets are T cells, the modified cells may recognize and destroy one another. This unintended attack can undermine the treatment.

Natural killer cells avoid this complication because they are a different type of immune cell. They can be programmed to attack harmful T cells without triggering the same problem of engineered T cells killing each other.

"NK cells can treat these T cell malignancies -- not only T cell cancer, but also T cell autoimmune diseases," Chen says.

Producing CAR NK cells outside the body, however, still requires much of the specialized equipment, labor, and processing associated with CAR T cell manufacturing. To overcome these limitations, the MIT team investigated whether NK cells could instead be engineered "in vivo," meaning directly inside the body.

"If a patient can just get an infusion of nanoparticles, it would dramatically simplify the process and reduce costs," Anderson says.

Although researchers are actively developing CAR NK cell therapies for cancer and autoimmune disorders, none have received FDA approval.

How mRNA Nanoparticles Reprogram Immune Cells

The MIT team designed lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) capable of transporting messenger RNA into natural killer cells. The mRNA carries instructions for producing a chimeric antigen receptor that directs the modified immune cell toward a specific target.

The technology can be adapted to recognize different proteins depending on the disease being treated. For example, the researchers can provide instructions for a receptor that recognizes CD19, a protein found on B cells, or CD3, a protein present on T cells, including those responsible for autoimmune attacks.

To help the nanoparticles reach the correct immune cells, the scientists covered their surfaces with antibody fragments. These fragments recognize and attach to receptors on NK cells, helping deliver the genetic instructions where they are needed.

Once inside an NK cell, the mRNA directs the production of the new receptor, giving the immune cell the ability to recognize and attack its intended target.

The researchers then tested whether this approach could efficiently reprogram NK cells and whether the resulting cells could combat cancer and autoimmune disease in mice.

Reprogrammed Immune Cells Eliminate Tumors in Mice

The initial experiments produced encouraging results. After injecting the nanoparticles into mice, the researchers successfully modified approximately 80 percent of the NK cells they were targeting.

They next investigated whether these engineered cells could attack tumors. In mice with an aggressive form of melanoma, three of the five animals treated with nanoparticles designed to direct NK cells against the cancer experienced complete remission.

The researchers also tested the technique against T cell lymphoma using humanized mice. These animals receive transfusions of human blood cells, temporarily giving them immune systems that share certain characteristics with those of humans.

In this model, the treatment produced substantial tumor destruction. After five injections of the nanoparticles, the tumors were completely eliminated.

Importantly, these results were comparable to those achieved with CAR NK cells produced through the more traditional method of collecting NK cells, modifying them outside the body, and then returning them to the animals.

This suggests that generating CAR NK cells directly inside the body could offer similar cancer-fighting capabilities while avoiding the complicated manufacturing process required by conventional cell therapies.

A Single Injection Reverses Autoimmune Liver Damage

The researchers also wanted to determine whether their technology could help treat autoimmune diseases, in which the immune system mistakenly damages healthy tissues.

They focused on autoimmune hepatitis, a condition in which abnormal T cells attack hepatocytes, the main functional cells of the liver. By designing nanoparticles that instruct NK cells to recognize these harmful T cells, the scientists tested whether they could interrupt the autoimmune response.

The treatment successfully eliminated the autoreactive T cells in mice with the disease. Even more encouragingly, the animals' damaged liver tissue healed after the harmful immune cells were removed.

These improvements occurred after just one nanoparticle injection, demonstrating the potential of the approach beyond cancer treatment.

"This study is an excellent example of the power of nano delivery systems and their ability to potentially treat cancer and other diseases," Langer says.

A New Direction for Cancer and Autoimmune Treatments

The researchers believe that reprogramming natural killer cells inside the body could eventually provide new treatment options for a much wider range of conditions.

Among the diseases they hope to target are multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis, both of which can involve harmful immune responses driven by dysfunctional T cells.

Although the findings are promising, the experiments were conducted in mice, and further research will be necessary to determine whether the technique is safe and effective in humans.

If successful, the technology could make engineered immune cell treatments considerably more accessible by replacing a lengthy laboratory manufacturing process with the direct delivery of genetic instructions through nanoparticles.

The research received funding from Sanofi, the Marble Center for Cancer Nanomedicine, and a Koch Institute Support (core) Grant from the National Cancer Institute.

#4335. The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – October 23, 2026

This week has been home to some disheartening news. BioWare, the creators of games like Mass Effect and Dragon Age, is being shut down amid a flurry of layoffs. It's another frustrating story from a struggling video game industry. Below you will find some of our stories about the legendary developer, including our massive 2016 oral history. And then after that, you can read about our recommendations of what to play this weekend.

I spent the early hours playing Final Fantasy Resonance trying to figure out precisely why I couldn't put it down. I eventually realized that the game manages in a very purposeful way to answer that quiet need I've so frequently had: "I wish I could experience a game just like Final Fantasy IV or VI again, for the first time, but with a new cast and story." That's pretty much what you can expect here; Resonance is a very purposeful throwback experience that harkens to the early days of FF pixel adventures, but with several modern conveniences, graphical flourishes, and depth added into the mix. It's a big and refreshingly wholesome journey of entertaining party members, summoning giant creatures, flying an airship across the world, and fighting turn-based battles that include absurd spell effects. It's one of my favorite games of the year, and well worth the time it will take to explore. Read our full review for more.

Expect to hear a lot of people proclaiming this as "one of the good ones," as Modern Warfare came out swinging this week with a strong campaign, compelling additions to competitive multiplayer, and an impressive extraction shooter mode in the form of DMZ. I've already been impressed by the first few hours of the campaign, which offers a tense, harrowing, and often disturbingly brutal story that bounces between a number of character perspectives. The gunplay feels tuned in, the traversal and melee is satisfying, and the narrative beats grounded in excellent actin performances. Our reviewer has spent even more time with the full game, and can share their full perspective to help inform whether you want to take a dive into this year's installment.

The Nintendo Sports franchise, which began with Wii Sports in 2006, has never been about the single-player experience. That remains true 20 years later in Nintendo Switch Sports Resort. But this time around, Nintendo has boosted the amount of content beyond what the series has typically provided, appealing to all player counts, all while retaining its trademark approachability. Whether you're joining together with three friends for some friendly competition across the package's 12 sports or you're trying to climb the Island Crown ladder by beating increasingly difficult single-player opponents, Switch Sports Resort is a great motion-controlled collection.

Halloween is around the corner. As you’re buying overpriced candy, deciding which version of the Joker to dress up as, and debating between watching Obsession and Backrooms over a cup of cider, it’s the perfect time to replay old horror games or dive into new ones. 2026 has a solid roster of choices for the latter thanks to releases like Resident Evil Requiem, Paranormasight: The Mermaid’s Curse, and Silent Hill: Townfall, but Tenebris Somnia shouldn’t be overlooked if you’re looking for a cool indie throwback.

Part retro-inspired adventure game, part live-action indie horror film, you’ll uncover the mystery of a nightmare-induced apartment building and battle horrors to rescue your trapped ex. The gameplay is survival horror 101, but it’s executed well, with consistently clever and inventive puzzle-solving as a highlight. It may not be a graphical powerhouse, but Tenebris Somnia still maintains a creepy atmosphere thanks to solid scares partly delivered by effective and well-made live-action cinematics. If you’re going to binge horror films, you may as well play one too. You can read my full review here.

Full disclosure: I have not played One Piece: Grand Gourmet. I was trying to finish up Castlevania: Belmont's Curse when a review game landed in my lap that I've had to give my full attention. That said, I have watched a lot of the One Piece anime, have a cat named Nami, and dog named Luffy.

I don't know if One Piece: Grand Gourmet is any good, but I like the premise and pixel graphics. One Piece is a very malleable franchise (which is why its live action adaptation is pretty good), so the idea of managing a restaurant as Sanji feels like it could be a very good fit. I plan on climbing aboard with all my hopes and dreams soon. And it is out now, which is good to know.

Similar to the entry above, I have not yet played Stupid Never Dies yet (there are too many video games!), but we like to use this weekly article to call out the new video games of the week. I am eager to check out Stupid Never Dies primarily because of its pop-punk soundtrack and 2000s aesthetic. I think it has the potential to be a fun, nostalgic throwback to my youth when I was learning Blink-182's "Dammit" on guitar and playing Devil May Cry.

The Blood of Dawnwalker has been out for just over seven weeks now, but I wouldn't blame you if you haven't finished it – or even started it – yet. A lot has come out! But if you need a reason to jump back in, this week's 1.1 update is a great excuse – the devs have added hundreds of bug fixes and other minor improvements, so it should run better than it ever did before. There's also an even easier difficulty mode if you want to cruise through without worrying about combat, and a new in-game potion that lets you respec all your skill points. I stalled out about halfway through (when I started playing Wolverine), but I'm planning to jump back in this weekend.

Oh, and you can pet dogs and cats now. Maybe I should have led with that.

Multiplayer physics mountain-climbing game Peak became one of the most viral co-op experiences of 2025 (I refuse to use the term friendslop), but only PC players have enjoyed its wacky shenanigans. That changed this week as Peak is now available on PS5, Xbox Series X/S, and Switch 2. Either alone or, preferably, alongside up to three friends, you’ll try to ascend procedurally generated, absurdly unrealistic mountains riddled with dangers. Working together is key, a tricky prospect thanks to the in-game proximity chat that necessitates sticking together, but griefing each other, intentionally or otherwise, is just as entertaining – maddeningly frustrating at times, but entertaining. Peak on consoles includes all post-launch content and, best of all, supports crossplay for all platforms.

The original Azul remains one of my all-time favorite games even after many years, but it just misses the bar with its strategic complexity to be one I'd pull out to play with the kids. That why I was especially delighted to find that Azul Kids is one of those rare "adapted for children" projects that turned out extremely well.

Players take on the roll of creative young artists building mosaic displays with various colored tiles. The concept remains simple enough to work for even very young players of age five or six, but the whole family should have fun with the approachable strategy implications of choosing tiles and completing your masterpiece.

#4334. Battlefield 6 Loses Court Case Over Ban

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

Account bans are a dangerous thing, especially for titles with a price tag. There’s a reason most games make you agree to terms of use before you get started playing online, clarifying bannable offenses and ensuring you know the groundwork you’re playing under. Without them, and without proper explanations for bans, companies can get into more than just PR trouble.

Modern Warfare 4's launch party is still going, with a free play period for DMZ ready to rake in new players.

Back in early August, a Battlefield 6 player named Rychadv complained on Reddit that his profile has been randomly, unexplainably banned after a period of inactivity, with no support levied from EA after attempts at appeal. Today, he revealed that he took EA to court over the case and won, regaining access to his account effective immediately.

While most don’t carefully read the terms and conditions many online games ask of you, the agreement does serve as somewhat legally binding, acting as a way for the studio running the game to establish when and if they can pull your plug. Cheating, improper communications use, or any step out of line with the terms laid out can be used as a justification to temporarily, or permanently, ban you.

The odd part that swung this case fully in Rychadv’s favor was the lack of an actual motive. For no discernible reason, after an extended break from the game, DICE had simply banned his account, with no means of reacquiring it or fighting the ban. Especially on a full-priced title like Battlefield 6, this type of hiccup is strictly unacceptable, potentially costing Rychadv a whole new copy if he didn’t drag DICE to court.

Bans need to be carefully considered by studios before they’re implemented; otherwise, they risk both stepping on toes and unjustly kicking out solid chunks of their populace. The threat of bans, more so than the bans themselves, is often enough to keep the problem children in line. We’ve all had a mouthy, rude player on the team, the more invested in the game they are, the less likely they are to get heinous.

Without them, and without proper explanations for bans, companies can get into more than just PR trouble.

This widely depends on both the player culture and ban frequency of the game itself, and is far more common in free-to-play titles where accounts can quickly rise and fall. For full-priced experiences, developers need to be a bit more careful with the ban hammer, and they especially need to make sure any perceived bannable offenses actually happened.

The gradual move away from physical media for the majority of the gaming industry makes the threat of random bans a bit more serious, especially with cases like Rychadv’s still out in the open. It’s not just multiplayer titles that are always online, and who's to say some studio couldn’t kick you out for what you do in a single-player game in the future, even when it's only affecting your copy?

This is definitely stepping into the speculative, but it's important to remember that digital titles aren’t really yours; you simply buy a license from the studio to play. Without the promise of physical media, there’s a certain formlessness to the games we buy, like they could slip away at any moment.

With no promise of actual ownership, situations like Rychadv’s could happen more and more, putting the onus of action onto the players to hold studios over the fire a bit. When you agree to the terms of service, make sure to read up on it. While you’re playing by the studio’s rules, they need to respect them as well, especially for titles with a price tag.

Improper use of bans could lead to more legal disputes like Rychadv’s, as players become more willing to hold studios to their word.

Deadlock is starting to suffer from the same fate as other free-to-play games, with bot farmers crawling from the woodwork.

#4333. Phantom Blade Zero Review In Progress – Shaping Up To Be One Of The Best Action Games I've Ever Played

Phantom Blade Zero is an astounding achievement for the action genre. So astounding that I feel pulled to experience everything it has to offer… and that means instead of rolling credits, I’ve been busy completing story-critical side quests and more to get the most complete ending. That’s another way of saying I am enjoying this game very, very much but still need more time to render a final verdict, which is why you’re reading a review-in-progress of Phantom Blade Zero rather than a scored piece.

Though I’m not interested in guesstimating a score right now, I know it will be high because Phantom Blade Zero impresses and then some. It is one of the best action games I’ve ever played, and I’m shocked to be writing that. This is a debut of sorts for developer S-Game, which has dabbled in mobile games and smaller-scale titles; it’s the team’s first triple-A release, and its first game of this kind. This studio is so clearly a dedicated student of the genre, analyzing what works here and what works there in other action greats to create something of its own. It looks forward at what action games can do, can play like, can look like, while looking back at the games before it and understanding why those games – games like Devil May Cry, Elden Ring, Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, Bayonetta, and just about every other quality action game you can think of – continue to be ones we hold so highly. Should it stick the landing, Phantom Blade Zero will join that echelon of action pedigree.

Protagonist Soul is a quiet, mostly stoic martial arts master who prefers to let his blades (of which there are so, so many) do the talking. The Order he’s sworn his life to betrays him, and, in an effort to right wrongs, he discovers a villainous conspiracy to seize full power of the blood-soaked Chinese martial underground known as Wulin. As a result, puppets, secret sects, powerful god-like creatures, monstrous beasts, and much more prowl Wulin’s various biomes. I haven’t kept count, but there are a massive number of enemies to take down, both standard mob variants and bosses, and the game stays fresh throughout. It's even fresher when you consider how many weapons you can acquire on Soul’s journey.

Every weapon is wholly unique, like picking up a new character in a fighting game, each with its own moveset and abilities. Upgrading these weapons through various tiers unlocks additional abilities, and you can even Soul Temper weapons to add one final, game-changing ability or perk. A fully upgraded weapon can have a moveset that uses the majority of buttons on your controller. You can do the same with Phantom Edges, special tide-turning weapons with limited uses (before you build up additional charges). Combined with different accessories and medicine types, Phantom Blade Zero offers hundreds, perhaps thousands, of combat kit permutations. You can play as a drunken fighter who switches between sober, tipsy, and drunken states, with his range and damage output changing as a result; you can focus on a bleed build, ripping enemies to shreds with charged attacks that utilize Soul's own HP to deal extra damage (that can then be earned back with bleed); you can use lightning, wind, fire, and ice to create elemental storms against enemies, and you can use a sword that switches between different elemental states on command as well. You can also just pound enemies to pulp with Phantom Edge fists, too. I’ve struggled to stop using these fists since acquiring them because they’re so satisfying.

Forty-plus hours into Phantom Blade Zero, it feels like I’ve played as dozens of different Souls because I've discovered so many build types. S-Game smartly pushes you to try new builds and weapons as you get them, doling out generous upgrade materials and currency; it encourages you to try everything, and the next weapon might just become your new favorite.

Finding these materials (and additional fights) is great fun, too, because Phantom Blade Zero’s various open-area biomes are a genuine joy to explore. You are always rewarded for taking the optional path, and those rewards are always worthwhile. You might find a healthy pile of upgrade materials, or a boss with a weapon you’ll fall in love with. The way buildings, alleys, caves, cliffsides, and other environmental features weave in and out of each other evokes FromSoftware’s architectural design and the subsequent shortcut “aha!” moments.

That said, Phantom Blade Zero is definitively not a Soulslike, though you’d be forgiven for assuming as much given its challenging suite of bosses, interconnected world, and Phantom Bell checkpoints, which are this game’s equivalent of bonfires. However, its challenge is much more surmountable (with various difficulties and accessories to ease parry and dodge timing), and its world progression is materially different. Kill an enemy and it’s dead for good, which to my surprise, adds a sense of worldbuilding I didn’t know I wanted. Progression through this journey feels tangible because I’m actually removing traces of evil with my weapons, traces that don’t respawn when I interact with checkpoints. It’s a nice change of pace that narratively speaks to Soul’s efforts.

Along the way, countless reading materials shed light on Phantom Blade Zero’s intertwining stories, and tracking down the next memory, scroll, or book entry rewards you if you’re interested in the full picture of this Wuxia story. I’d argue the game’s story is its weakest element, but only when compared to the rest of the package. It doesn't break any new ground narratively, but it provides enough mystery and thrill to keep things moving. And while performances are great, talking to characters is still mostly just two people standing across from each other talking through a new quest. Fortunately, cutscenes pick up the slack with dramatic villains, heartfelt revelations, raw tension, and more.

Production value is high across the board, thanks to incredibly impressive animation and a beautiful rendering of this dark fantasy China. Faces are lifelike, nudging up just shy of the uncanny valley as close-ups reveal porous details, lip quivers, and more, bringing an excellent cast of Chinese performances to life. The English voice acting has its standouts, but Soul’s voice is boring, so I highly recommend the Chinese vocals.

Boss fights draw clear inspiration from Chinese cinema and boast a wondrous sense of awe and scale that only the best in the genre typically offer. There are a ton of bosses, too, with very few repeats (repeats do happen in segmented challenge trials), and it’s impressive to think back on just how many I defeated, and just how many of them delivered a unique fight. I appreciate the checkpoints between boss phases as well. There are so many bosses – nearing 100 or more if I had to guess – and having my progression saved through phases removes some of the repetition I often feel when, say, phase two of a boss continues to kill me and I have to blitz through phase one again and again before taking another stab at it.

That scale and on-screen excitement carry through almost every fight in the game, down to even the simplest mob fights, though these are starting to feel a touch repetitive as I’m barreling toward the game’s end. Soul moves like the world’s greatest martial artist, but your controller inputs make it happen. If you mash the attack button, it looks nice… but if you use each weapon’s prescribed inputs and abilities, Phantom Blade Zero delivers a level of detailed action I’ve seen in few other games. You direct the game’s action, and this lets you turn what might otherwise be just another group of fodder enemies into an electric bout of spectacle.

To say I greatly enjoy this game greatly undersells my feelings – writing this review-in-progress is frustrating because I want to get back to Phantom Blade Zero. I expect to reach credits in the coming days, so please be on the lookout for my final verdict this week.

#4329. A 24-hour fast triggers a surprising repair response in the gut

A 24-hour fast may help prepare the intestines to recover from radiation damage, but scientists have discovered that a particular gut bacterium plays a crucial role in making this possible. New preclinical research from The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center reveals how fasting and beneficial microbes work together to activate the body's natural tissue repair mechanisms.

The findings could eventually lead to new ways to protect healthy tissue during cancer treatment. By improving the intestine's ability to recover from radiation exposure, researchers hope to reduce serious side effects and potentially make radiation therapy safer and more effective.

Published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the study was co-led by Helen Piwnica-Worms, Ph.D., professor of Experimental Radiation Oncology, and Kunal Rai, Ph.D., professor of Genomic Medicine.

"Fasting helps prepare intestinal cells to respond more quickly and effectively after injury, almost like training the cells with an emergency preparedness plan," Piwnica-Worms said. "This study helps explain how that plan is organized and identifies a key bacterium involved in coordinating the response."

Why Radiation Therapy Can Damage the Intestines

Radiation therapy is widely used to treat cancers in the abdomen, including pancreatic, colorectal, and gynecologic cancers. Although radiation can destroy cancer cells, it can also harm nearby healthy tissue. The small intestine is particularly vulnerable because its delicate lining is highly sensitive to radiation exposure.

When this protective lining becomes damaged, patients may experience nausea, diarrhea, and infections. Severe injuries can cause life-threatening complications. These risks can also restrict the amount of radiation doctors can safely administer, potentially limiting treatment options.

Previous preclinical research from the Piwnica-Worms Laboratory showed that fasting before radiation exposure helped the intestines recover afterward. However, researchers had not fully determined why going without food produced this protective effect.

The latest study provides an important piece of that puzzle by identifying a specific gut bacterium and explaining how it helps intestinal cells prepare for injury.

Researchers found that 24 hours of fasting increased the abundance of a beneficial bacterium called Akkermansia muciniphila, also known as AKK, in the small intestine. This microbe produces a substance called propionate, which helps trigger changes inside intestinal cells that make them better prepared to regenerate following radiation damage.

Propionate works alongside other metabolic changes caused by fasting to modify proteins known as histones. These proteins serve as structures around which DNA is packaged inside cells. Small chemical markers added to histones can influence which genes become active without changing the underlying DNA sequence.

These modifications make portions of DNA more accessible, allowing cells to activate genes involved in tissue regeneration. During fasting, a population of intestinal cells carrying these repair programs becomes more abundant.

In effect, fasting helps prepare these cells with the biological instructions they will need if an injury occurs. When the intestines are subsequently exposed to radiation, the prepared cells can expand and help rebuild the damaged intestinal lining.

One Gut Bacterium Proves Essential for Recovery

To determine how important AKK was to this process, the researchers selectively removed the bacterium. Without it, fasting no longer produced the same regenerative benefits.

Even more revealing, the protective response returned only when the bacterium was restored in combination with fasting. This demonstrated that neither component alone was sufficient to reproduce the full effect observed in the study.

The results suggest that fasting does more than temporarily change the gut's metabolism. Together with AKK, it alters the activity of intestinal cells before radiation exposure, placing them in a state that supports more efficient recovery after damage occurs.

By uncovering this connection between nutrition, gut bacteria, and cellular regeneration, the researchers have identified a potential new way to strengthen the body's response to tissue injury. The discovery could be especially valuable for protecting healthy organs during cancer treatment.

Could Gut Bacteria Make Cancer Treatment Safer?

Although the results are promising, the research remains preclinical. Additional studies will be needed to determine whether the same protective mechanism operates in humans and whether it can safely improve outcomes for patients receiving radiation therapy.

One possibility is that the newly discovered pathway could be used to help other healthy tissues recover from cancer treatment. Researchers are particularly interested in tissues with rapidly dividing cells, including bone marrow, which can also suffer treatment-related damage.

If further investigations support the findings, clinical trials could eventually explore whether activating this repair mechanism benefits patients undergoing abdominal radiation therapy.

Importantly, the discovery may also provide ways to achieve these effects without requiring patients to fast. Treatments involving beneficial bacteria or the molecules they produce could potentially stimulate similar repair processes while avoiding the practical difficulties of food restriction during cancer care.

"Fasting is not always practical for cancer patients, and this work supports several other potential ways to enhance recovery after treatment," Rai said. "Whether through dietary interventions, targeted microbes or their metabolites, the goal is to help repair healthy tissue more effectively while patients receive the cancer therapies they need."

The research was funded by the National Cancer Institute (NCI) within the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the Cancer Prevention and Research Institute of Texas (CPRIT).

#4327. Battlefield 6’s first big map in months is coming to Labs soon, but I'm more excited about BF4's Golmud Railway making its way to BF6

As promised, Battlefield Labs is coming back to bring us a preview of some of Battlefield 6’s upcoming Season 2 content.

Battlefield 6’s Season 2 was recently pushed back by a month to give Battlefield Studios time to polish up its content. Now, the developer has revealed how it plans to use some of that time, and the first port of call is Battlefield Labs.

As discussed in the initial delay message, BF Studios wants the community’s involvement earlier and more consistently in the development of future content. This includes Season 2, of course, and a big component of what it’s bringing to the game is headed to Labs.

The first Battlefield Labs session kicking off soon will focus on Contaminated, one of the new maps coming to Battlefield 6 with Season 2. BF Studios says the map falls between Eastwood and Mirak Valley, in terms of size.

The blog post even likened it to Battlefield 1’s St. Quentin Scar, and Battlefield 5’s Arras. Although we’ve yet to actually play it, the size and description do sound really well, especially in a game as starved of big maps as Battlefield 6 currently is.

Another thing BF Studios wants to test is the way ground vehicle gameplay and aerial presence interact with infantry combat, which is pretty standard for most Battlefield maps. Interestingly, there appears to be some sort of mechanic unique to Contaminated that the developer also wants to evaluate.

More Labs sessions are planned, including one that will show off new gameplay tools and vehicles. The AH-6 Little Bird helicopter was specifically namedropped, which makes sense given that it’s going to be part of Season 2’s content.

Battlefield Labs sessions will also extend beyond the biggest-ticket items of maps and vehicles. BF Studios said we should expect tests of upcoming features, like the Aircraft Radar, as part of a list of other air combat updates.

Ground vehicles, and they way the various rockets interact with them, will also be evaluated in a different session, with specific adjustments planned for RPGs and TOWs. And, of course, the work to improve and perfect hit reg remains ongoing, and future tweaks will go through Labs first.

There’s even more exciting news for fans of big maps, as the blog post also confirmed that Battlefield 4’s Golmud Railway is currently in the works, planned to go live in a future season. Golmud Railway will show up early in Labs, and you can expect it to evolve over multiple sessions.

For context, when it does arrive in Battlefield 6, Golmud Railway will be the largest map in the game, which is saying something. Though the map is beloved by vehicle players, it has its issues elsewhere, and BF Studios says it will be looking at all that when it creates the BF6, emphasising that it won’t be a simple port of the BF4 original.

Finally, the post throws a bone to Redsec battle royale players still waiting for a Solo mode. BF Studios continues to test the idea internally, but it’s taking a while. Needless to say, there are so many aspects that need to be considered. Game pace, balance, player survivability, match flow just to name a few.

Redsec BR was built with squads in mind, so that task is extra challenging. Though the developer didn’t say when we can expect Solos to arrive in Labs, players will get a chance to experience it before it enters the live game.

#4325. For decades, we were told to avoid full-fat dairy. New research says otherwise

For years, people have been encouraged to choose low-fat or fat-free dairy products to protect their hearts and manage their weight. But growing scientific evidence suggests that full-fat dairy may not carry the health risks many have come to expect.

A new Canadian study led by University of Toronto professor Harvey Anderson adds to that evidence. Researchers found that adults who consumed three servings of full-fat dairy each day for 12 weeks did not experience harmful changes in body weight, body composition, energy metabolism, or blood cholesterol levels compared with participants following a diet containing little dairy.

Even more surprisingly, participants who consumed more dairy showed improvements in blood pressure and obtained greater amounts of several important nutrients.

The findings, published in The Journal of Nutrition, raise new questions about longstanding dietary recommendations and suggest that the health effects of dairy may be more complicated than its saturated fat content alone would indicate.

For decades, nutrition guidelines in Canada and many other countries have recommended choosing low-fat or fat-free milk, yogurt, and other dairy products. The main concern has been saturated fat, which can raise levels of LDL cholesterol in the blood.

Often called "bad" cholesterol, LDL can contribute to fatty deposits in the arteries. Over time, this buildup can increase the risk of heart attacks, strokes, and other cardiovascular problems.

Because full-fat dairy contains more saturated fat than reduced-fat alternatives, health authorities have traditionally encouraged people to limit their intake.

However, research examining what happens when people actually consume full-fat dairy has produced a more complicated picture.

Anderson, a professor of nutritional sciences at the University of Toronto's Temerty Faculty of Medicine, points out that numerous studies involving humans have failed to find a clear association between full-fat dairy consumption and poor health outcomes.

Other research has even identified potential protective effects. That includes a recent study led by Temerty Medicine professor Kozeta Milliku, which found an association between whole-fat milk consumption and a lower risk of childhood obesity.

These findings have prompted scientists to investigate whether dairy foods behave differently in the body than their individual nutrients might suggest.

What Happened When Adults Ate Full-Fat Dairy Every Day?

To explore the question, Anderson and his colleagues conducted a 12-week study involving 74 adults with overweight or obesity.

Participants were randomly assigned to one of three dietary approaches. The first group followed a calorie-restricted diet containing little dairy. The second consumed three daily servings of dairy while maintaining an energy-neutral diet, meaning their calorie intake was intended to match the energy their bodies used. The third also consumed three servings of dairy each day but otherwise ate without specific calorie restrictions.

All participants received guidance based on Canada's food guide, and the researchers supplied full-fat dairy products during the study.

At the end of 12 weeks, the team compared several measures of metabolic health, including body weight, body composition, and cholesterol levels.

The results challenged expectations. Participants who consumed three servings of dairy daily did not show meaningful differences in weight gain, body composition, or blood cholesterol compared with those who ate little dairy.

The higher-dairy groups also experienced improvements in blood pressure and consumed more calcium, protein, and vitamin D. These nutrients play essential roles in maintaining healthy bones, supporting muscle function, and regulating numerous processes throughout the body.

"Those that had three servings of dairy didn't have adverse levels of blood cholesterol or lipids or evidence of insulin resistance," says Anderson.

Blood lipids are fats and fat-like substances circulating in the bloodstream, including cholesterol and triglycerides. Insulin resistance occurs when the body's cells become less responsive to insulin, making it harder to regulate blood sugar and increasing the risk of type 2 diabetes.

Although the results are encouraging, the study was relatively small and lasted only three months. Longer and larger studies are needed to determine whether the findings translate into lasting health benefits or changes in cardiovascular disease risk.

Why might full-fat dairy have different health effects than researchers would predict from its saturated fat content?

One possible explanation is the dairy matrix hypothesis, an idea that emphasizes how the physical structure of food influences the way the body processes its nutrients.

Rather than treating milk, cheese, or yogurt as simple collections of fat, protein, vitamins, and minerals, this theory considers how those components interact within the food itself.

"With dairy products, it's got two proteins -- casein and whey -- that are bound together with fat and with nutrients mixed in," says Anderson.

Casein and whey are the two major types of protein found in milk. Both provide amino acids that the body uses to build and maintain tissues, but they are digested and absorbed at different rates.

According to Anderson, the complex arrangement of proteins, fats, and other nutrients in dairy products can help regulate how quickly those nutrients are released during digestion.

This means the body's response to eating a whole dairy food may differ from its response to consuming an equivalent amount of saturated fat on its own.

The broader implication is that a food's health effects cannot always be predicted by examining a single ingredient. Its structure, nutritional composition, and interactions among nutrients may all matter.

Why the Findings Could Be Important for Older Adults

The researchers believe these results could be particularly relevant for older people, who often need to obtain sufficient protein and essential nutrients while consuming fewer calories.

As people age, their overall energy requirements frequently decrease. However, maintaining muscle mass, bone strength, and other important bodily functions still requires adequate nutrition.

That can make it difficult to meet nutritional needs, particularly for people with smaller appetites.

Anderson explains that dairy products offer a familiar, convenient source of concentrated nutrition. They provide protein, calcium, and other nutrients in foods that many older adults already enjoy and regularly consume.

The new findings suggest that including full-fat dairy in a balanced diet may help people meet these nutritional requirements without necessarily worsening cholesterol levels or markers associated with diabetes risk.

However, the study did not directly establish whether long-term consumption prevents or increases diabetes, heart disease, or other chronic conditions.

Rethinking Nutrition Advice Beyond Individual Nutrients

Beyond the debate over dairy fat, the research highlights a broader challenge in nutrition science: judging the health effects of entire foods rather than focusing exclusively on individual nutrients.

Traditional dietary advice has often emphasized reducing specific components, such as saturated fat. Although these recommendations are grounded in evidence about cardiovascular risk, researchers increasingly recognize that different foods containing the same nutrients may not have identical effects on health.

The University of Toronto findings contribute to this discussion by showing that full-fat dairy can be incorporated into certain diets without the unfavorable short-term metabolic changes that might be expected from its saturated fat content.

That does not mean saturated fat is harmless or that everyone should switch to full-fat dairy. Instead, it suggests that the overall food, its nutritional structure, and the broader dietary pattern deserve consideration.

For people trying to navigate changing nutrition recommendations and conflicting health messages, Anderson favors a practical approach rather than complicated dietary rules.

"Keep it simple, eat a variety of foods and not too much of anything."

This research was supported by Dairy Research Cluster 3 under the Canadian Agricultural Partnership AgriScience Program, and the Mitacs Accelerate program.

#4324. Grammy Award-Winning Composer Austin Wintory Shares His Early Musical Drafts Intended For Mass Effect 5

Last week, EA shut down Mass Effect and Dragon Age developer BioWare, which resulted in the cancellation of the fifth Mass Effect game that was announced in 2020. As the fallout from this closure settles, famed video game composer Austin Wintory has shared that he'd been working on a potential soundtrack for the now-canceled game and has publicly released early versions of this score.

In a Bluesky thread, Wintory, who has composed soundtracks for games such as Journey, Sword of the Sea (for which he won a Grammy), Assassin’s Creed: Syndicate, and The Banner Saga trilogy, writes, “Mass Effect was my ultimate white whale, my all-time dream project. For the last couple years I'd been in discussion w/ BioWare & EA to take on the project & as part of that I wrote close to 20 minutes of music to explore where the franchise can go next, may as well share it!"

Wintory uploaded a 20-minute video consisting of eight tracks to his YouTube channel. The video begins with a message further elaborating on the partnership between BioWare, EA, and him. “For the past several years, I’d been in dialogue with people both at BioWare and EA to potentially jump into Mass Effect 5. As part of these conversations, I decided to surprise the team by writing/recording a gigantic love letter to the franchise, with my idea of where it can go next.”

Wintory adds that he composed the music in 2025 and that he “knew nothing” about what Mass Effect 5's story entailed when he did. As such, he describes the music as “narratively speculative.” He adds that this conceptual soundtrack was a direct homage to Jack Wall and Sam Hulick’s soundtrack on the first Mass Effect “while leaning even harder on true analog synths, and a more complex integration of the orchestra (almost akin to the hybrid nature of The Matrix),” he writes. Each music track features a message by Wintory explaining his inspiration for its production.

“Receiving the news alongside everyone else that EA had decided to not only cancel the project but shutdown BioWare entirely was a deeply felt loss," Wintory writes in the video's description. "It's been hard to see dear friends lose their jobs, and this beloved franchise seemingly vanish forever. Thank you nonetheless to everyone at BioWare and EA's music department for gifting me the chance to dream in your sandbox. It was a privilege to do even that much.”

Wintory's music is the latest piece of potential Mass Effect 5 content to emerge since BioWare’s closure. A day after the shutdown announcement, an unreleased but reportedly legitimate cinematic trailer for the canceled Mass Effect leaked online.

#4322. Free-To-Play MOBA Pokémon Unite Is Shutting Down In March

The free-to-play MOBA Pokémon Unite will shut down in March, over five years after its 2021 launch. Although a gradual suspension of services begins today, fans will enjoy one last hurrah thanks to a big in-game event running for the remainder of the game’s lifecycle.

Launched in July 2021 for Switch before migrating to iOS and Android later that year, Pokémon Unite was billed as a friendlier take on the MOBA genre popularized by Dota 2 and League of Legends, thanks to its short matches (10 minutes) and simplified mechanics. Despite its initial popularity, the game is winding down and will go offline for good on March 23, 2027.

An End of Service notice on the game’s website reads,

“We offer our sincerest gratitude to the many Trainers who have played since service started for the Nintendo Switch version on July 21, 2021. We would like to express our thanks to everyone by holding a special event until service ends. The Pokémon Unite Aeos Crown 2027 Tokyo competitive tournament (an event for Pokémon Unite only) will also be held as previously announced. We hope you continue to enjoy Pokémon Unite until the final day of service. After service ends, the 'Pokémon Unite Game Content Guidelines for Online Platforms' will no longer be published or maintained, and we will no longer provide support regarding use of Pokémon Unite videos and images.”

As of today, in-game sales of Aeos gems and Unite Club memberships/renewals have been suspended. Existing Unite Club members will continue to use their benefits until the end of the membership period.

On November 12, an update will kick off the aforementioned final special event, where players can obtain items such as all Unite licenses and Holoware that have appeared in the game up to that point. A library feature will also be added, letting players view certain records and in-game content even after the game shuts down on March 23. Those who don’t download the library feature before the shutdown date will not be able to get it afterward.

Qualifiers for the Aeos Crown 2027 Tokyo Competitive tournament will take place as planned on December 5. After the game shuts down on March 23, players won't be able to log in to Pokémon Unite or play any battles. Only the library feature will remain accessible.

We enjoyed Pokémon Unite when it launched, with executive video editor Alex Van Aken scoring it an 8 out of 10 in his review, writing, “The game eats away the hours of my day as I reassuringly say to myself, 'Just one more match.' Battles play out with the spectacle that the Pokémon series is known for, and with so many abilities to choose from, no match feels the same as the last. The game’s simple mechanics and recognizable characters make for an approachable MOBA experience, and with a potential catalog of nearly 900 Pokémon to pick from, my hopes are high for the future of Pokémon Unite.”

#4321. Arc Raiders finally reveals early 2026 roadmap, but we’re not getting a new map for a while

The first couple of months of 2026 in the world of Arc Raiders look pretty promising, but the big guns are being held back for now.

After weeks of waiting, Arc Raiders developer Embark has officially unveiled the first few months of the game’s 2026 roadmap. The plan is split into four months, covering January to April, collectively dubbed Escalation.

We’re expecting a content update each month, with the majority of the biggest additions happening on the game’s existing maps. There is, however, at least one new map in the works, but it won’t be here until sometime in April.

While we wait for that, Arc Raiders is going to go through several events and other in-game changes, some more meaningful (and exciting) than others. January looks to be the lightest so far, which makes sense given that it’s just a week or so from ending.

January’s chapter is titled Headwinds, kicking off on January 27. This segment will see the addition of a new matchmaking option for players above level 40 - at or near the game’s endgame. We’re also expecting a new Map Condition, and a new Player Project for everyone to contribute to.

Things start getting interesting in February, when Shrouded Sky will begin. This chapter brings three exciting additions to Arc Raiders. There will be a new Map Condition, new Arc Threat, and the start of another Player Project.

Interestingly, we’re going to see some sort of map update during the month, but Embark didn’t share anymore details. The next Raider Deck will also deploy in February, alongside a new Expedition Window.

The Flashpoint chapter begins in March, when we’re expecting another new Map Condition, one more new Arc Threat, as well as another Player Project. March’s most interesting addition is an update to everyone’s trusty rooster friend, Scrappy.

Finally, April is when the big guns come out, because that’s when the first new map of 2026 will arrive in Arc Raiders. With it, comes a new large Arc, which is to be expected. A new Map Condition will debut then, too, likely starting off on the new map.

That’s pretty much it, but seeing as we’re just one day away from the start of the January stage, things are about to get exciting again in Arc Raiders.

#4320. 8 Nintendo Titles That Should Get The Ocarina of Time Remake Treatment

Aden Carter is a Contributor at DualShockers who has been covering games professionally since 2020. He specializes in lists and guides, with a focus on RPGs, horror games, survival horror, Soulslikes, cozy/sim games, and action-adventure titles. Before joining DualShockers, Aden contributed to GameRant, XDA, Gamepur, I

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is one of the most beloved games ever created. Fans of this game talk about it with passion, remembering it as a key part of their childhood. The remake shows that fans still love this title, even almost 30 years after the original’s release. It also introduces new features and controls.

Of course, this isn’t the only game that Nintendo has ever made. Nintendo is known for creating many timeless games that fans continue to go back to year after year.

While they may not be as beloved as Ocarina of Time, these games definitely deserve to get the same treatment, breathing new life into them.

Super Mario Sunshine is one of those Nintendo titles that divides fans. There are many who love it, but then there are many who criticize the title for various reasons. Some of the reasons include the messy controls, and the dislike of using FLUDD constantly.

However, there is a large fanbase who misses this game - and I am not just saying that because it is one of my favorite Mario games. I’ve talked to many people who have said that they would love to see a full remake of Super Mario Sunshine.

Plus, remaking the game would allow Nintendo to fix some of the issues that it has. The team could make FLUDD more entertaining to use, fix the messy controls, and update the core gameplay to better fit the newer Mario titles.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time may be the most beloved Zelda title out there, but The Legend of Zelda: Majora’s Mask is a close second, with many fans saying they love it almost as much as Ocarina of Time.

Majora’s Mask is the edgy older brother of Ocarina of Time, giving players a darker story that is full of twists and turns. Plus, it is a direct sequel to Ocarina of Time, so it feels like a no-brainer to continue making remakes by giving Majora’s Mask the treatment given to its little brother.

After seeing Ocarina of Time in this new light, fans would go crazy if they could play the game’s sequel shortly after. There are plenty of other Zelda games worth revisiting, too.

The remake's dev team included younger folks, several of whom never played the original Ocarina of Time, who provided a much-needed modern view of things.

If there are two Pokémon games that I hear mentioned all the time, they are Pokémon Colosseum and Pokémon XD: Gale of Darkness. Gale of Darkness is the one I played a lot as a child, and is also typically the one I hear people talk about more.

Of course, both of these games deserve the Ocarina of Time treatment, but I think that Gale of Darkness deserves it a bit more. This game is one of the best Pokémon spin-offs, with it focusing on an evil organization that is creating shadow Pokémon.

More importantly, they created a Shadow Lugia and want to take over the world. Along with an actual evil organization, the game features a fun battle system that could use some updating to make it more modern. Plus, they could add all of the Pokémon to the game to make things more interesting.

Back in the days of the GameBoy Color, there were two titles that were ahead of their time. I am, of course, referring to The Legend of Zelda: Oracle of Ages and Oracle of Seasons. Both were fantastic titles for the time.

The best part about them is that they were linked together, expanding the story for those who played through both of them. When you beat one, you got a password. When you typed that password into the other game, it linked the two. When you beat the second title, it gives you a password to take back into the first game. This allows you to get the true ending.

It was an interesting mechanic that games didn’t typically do back then. Now, if Nintendo brings these titles back, makes them 3D or HD-2D, then the fan base would go wild and buy both of them. Plus, new technology means you can link the saves without the need of a password.

Eiji Aonuma and the development team for the Ocarina of Time remake discussed how one of the original's infamous dungeons is being improved.

One of the classic platformers from the N64 era is none other than Donkey Kong 64. It is a beloved title that could seriously use updating. After all, the Nintendo 64 wasn’t known for being the smoothest gameplay, and that is prevalent with DK64.

Despite the clunkiness, there is a huge soft spot for this title, and it is one that brings the entire crew together, allowing you to play as DK, Diddy, Lanky, Chunky, and more.

Nintendo brought back the idea of Donkey Kong being in a 3D platformer with Donkey Kong Bananza in June 2025, and it sold decently well, revealing that players still enjoy seeing this ape in his own games. If Nintendo wants to keep bringing back the classics, then this should be a serious consideration.

Earthbound is not a game that I personally grew up with, but it is one that I have always been told to try, and one that I know means a lot to the Nintendo fan base. I’ve met individuals who play it on a yearly basis because of how much they love it. It remains one of the memorable SNES role-playing games.

With all that being said, the game could use some serious updating. Its old-school RPG turn-based combat doesn’t hold up to today’s standard. Imagine if Nintendo gave this game the HD-2D treatment, or even decided to make the game fully 3D.

Either way, it would look fantastic, and it would mean the world to those who grew up with this beloved title and played it since then.

The first of the Fire Emblem games to be released in the west was simply titled Fire Emblem, but it is also known as Fire Emblem: The Blazing Blade, and it follows the story of Lyn, Eliwood, and Hector.

I remember getting this game as a child and falling in love with it. Since then, Fire Emblem has become one of my favorite game series from Nintendo. There are many who say that Path of Radiance is their favorite game, and it holds up well, but if Nintendo is going to go down the remake route, I think it would be best to start with the first game that was brought over to the west. This is just one highlight of many excellent Fire Emblem games.

The Fire Emblem series has seen some great success, with the latest of the games - Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave - selling over 1.3 million copies in a month. It is a series that has been beloved for decades, and it deserves to see one of the earlier titles brought back in either HD-2D or full 3D like the modern games.

There is no doubt that one of the most popular games Nintendo has ever made is Super Mario 64, and it has a special place in history. This game set the standards for movement and camera control in a 3D space.

Super Mario 64 is one of the most well-known games that was released on the N64, with it only being second to maybe Ocarina of Time. Not only that, but it inspired multiple games that came after.

If there is any game that Nintendo has created outside of The Legend of Zelda series that deserves a full remake with modernized graphics, it would be Super Mario 64. Almost any fan of Nintendo would say that a remake of this game would be a no-brainer.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is one of the most beloved games of all time, but these remakes might be just as meaningful to fans.

#4318. When your gut bacteria run out of fiber, they may start eating your gut lining

Eating more plants is widely associated with better health, but scientists are still uncovering exactly why. New research suggests that fiber is only part of the story. Certain plant proteins that resist digestion may also play a surprisingly important role in shaping gut bacteria and determining whether they produce beneficial or potentially harmful substances.

Plant-based diets support digestive health, immune function, metabolism, and cardiovascular health. One reason is that they help maintain a diverse community of microorganisms in the intestines, collectively known as the gut microbiome. Many of these bacteria are beneficial, helping break down food components that the human digestive system cannot process on its own.

Fiber is particularly important because it provides food for gut microbes. Plants also contain phytochemicals, natural substances that often give fruits and vegetables their vibrant colors and help protect them from environmental threats. These compounds can also contribute to human health. Yet researchers have only begun to understand the complicated chemical interactions that occur when gut bacteria digest plant foods.

Two studies led by Jenna AbuSalim and Joshua Rabinowitz, director of the Princeton Branch of the Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research, provide important new insights. One, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, shows how plant fiber and certain proteins influence gut bacteria to favor the production of beneficial compounds over potentially harmful ones. The other, published in Nature Metabolism in June, challenges the longstanding belief that many important chemical compounds circulating in the body originate exclusively from intestinal microbes.

"There's growing interest across medical disciplines in manipulating the human microbiome or using its metabolic products themselves for therapy," said Rabinowitz. "Diet holds great promise for controlling the microbiome and its outputs. But to devise effective therapeutic interventions, we need to understand what aspects of the diet control which microbial outputs."

How Plant Foods Change the Chemicals Your Gut Produces

In the PNAS study, researchers examined a group of substances called phenol metabolites. Metabolites are chemicals formed when the body or microorganisms break down and process nutrients. Some are essential for normal biological functions, while others can contribute to health problems when they accumulate.

The phenol metabolites investigated by the team are produced when gut bacteria process two amino acids, tyrosine and phenylalanine. Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins, but the compounds they ultimately produce can have very different effects on health.

Two metabolites derived from phenylalanine, phenylpropionate and hippuric acid, are associated with healthy body weight and better gut health. In contrast, two compounds derived from tyrosine, p-cresol sulfate and phenol sulfate, have been linked to worse outcomes in cancer patients and harmful effects throughout the body in people with kidney disease.

The researchers wanted to understand whether different components of plant foods could influence which of these substances gut microbes produce.

"Our studies showed that both the fiber and indigestible proteins from plants -- which we call 'proteins imitating fiber,' or Prif -- shift the balance of phenol metabolites from the harmful kind made from tyrosine to the healthful variety derived from phenylalanine," said AbuSalim.

An Overlooked Plant Protein Works Alongside Fiber

Although the health benefits of dietary fiber have been studied extensively, scientists have paid much less attention to plant proteins that pass through the digestive system without being fully broken down.

The researchers found that these indigestible proteins, which they call Prif, can reach the gut microbiome and serve as material for bacterial metabolism. In doing so, they influence which microbes thrive and which chemical compounds are produced.

Importantly, these proteins do not work in isolation. They cooperate with plant fiber to change how gut bacteria process nutrients, shifting their activity toward the production of beneficial phenol metabolites.

This discovery suggests that the nutritional value of plant foods may depend on more than their familiar concentrations of fiber, vitamins, and minerals. The amount and type of protein that escapes digestion could also help determine how food influences the gut microbiome.

When Gut Bacteria Run Low on Fiber, They May Feed on Your Gut's Protective Mucus

One of the most intriguing findings concerns where gut bacteria obtain the raw materials used to produce harmful metabolites.

To investigate, the researchers labeled proteins with stable (non-radioactive) isotopes, allowing them to track exactly where the proteins traveled and how they were processed in the digestive systems of mice. This technique works by giving molecules a detectable chemical signature without making them radioactive.

The experiments revealed an important difference between the sources of beneficial and harmful phenols.

The potentially harmful phenols came from gut bacteria breaking down proteins belonging to the host, including proteins found in the mucus layer that coats the intestines. This protective mucus helps separate intestinal microbes from the cells lining the gut and forms part of the body's natural defenses.

Meanwhile, the beneficial phenols were produced almost entirely from indigestible proteins supplied by food.

Fiber helped suppress the bacterial breakdown of the gut's protective mucus, reducing the production of harmful phenols. The indigestible plant proteins (Prif), in turn, supplied more dietary protein to gut bacteria, encouraging them to produce beneficial compounds instead.

Together, the findings reveal two complementary ways plant foods can influence intestinal chemistry. Fiber helps discourage bacteria from consuming proteins in the gut's protective mucus, while Prif provides an alternative source of nutrients that supports the production of healthier metabolites.

"We think Prifs represent an emerging class of dietary nutrients that shape the composition of the gut microbiome and could have a far-reaching influence on metabolic health," said AbuSalim.

The implications could eventually extend to nutrition labels and dietary recommendations.

"Food packaging may eventually list Prif right below fiber," said Rabinowitz.

A Second Discovery Challenges What Scientists Thought About Gut Bacteria

The companion study in Nature Metabolism addressed another important question: Are gut bacteria really responsible for producing all the metabolites traditionally attributed to them?

Along with phenol metabolites, the researchers examined indole metabolites, which are formed from tryptophan, another amino acid found in dietary proteins.

These substances have attracted considerable scientific interest because they participate in biological processes linked to inflammation, immune activity, and disease. Researchers have investigated their involvement in inflammatory bowel disease, neurodegenerative disorders, and cancer. Some indole metabolites have also been found to influence the spread of cancer and the immune system's ability to attack tumors.

Scientists have generally assumed that gut bacteria are the source of these compounds. That belief has encouraged efforts to develop probiotics and dietary interventions that increase the production of potentially beneficial indole metabolites.

However, this approach depends on an important assumption: that intestinal microbes are responsible for producing most or all of the compounds researchers want to influence.

If the body's own cells make substantial amounts of these metabolites, changing the microbiome may not be the most effective way to control their levels.

Your Body Can Make Compounds Once Attributed to Gut Microbes

To investigate, the research team used isotope tracing in mice, rats, and human cells to follow how different metabolites were produced.

The results challenged conventional thinking. Mammalian cells were capable of generating numerous phenol and indole metabolites independently of intestinal bacteria.

Among these were indole-3-lactate and indole-3-acetate, two biologically important compounds previously considered products of microbial metabolism.

The researchers also examined what happened when antibiotics disrupted the intestinal microbiome. If certain metabolites depended entirely on gut bacteria, their concentrations would be expected to decline sharply when those bacteria were depleted.

But many metabolites remained at substantial levels in the blood of antibiotic-treated mice. A similar pattern appeared in samples from patients receiving antibiotics, including people undergoing cancer treatment.

Other compounds behaved differently. Levels of indole-3-propionate and p-cresol sulfate, which are produced exclusively by microbes, declined following antibiotic treatment.

These results provided further evidence that some metabolites depend on intestinal bacteria, while others can also be manufactured by the body's own metabolic processes.

The distinction matters because it could change how researchers develop treatments intended to increase beneficial metabolites or reduce harmful ones.

What These Discoveries Mean for Nutrition and Future Treatments

Together, the two studies offer a more detailed understanding of how diet, gut microbes, and the body's own metabolism interact.

The first identifies an overlooked category of plant proteins that works with fiber to influence bacterial activity, potentially helping shift the balance away from harmful metabolic products. The second demonstrates that the body itself can produce many compounds once believed to originate exclusively from gut bacteria.

Both findings have implications for research into metabolic disease, digestive health, cancer, and other conditions involving the microbiome.

They also suggest that attempts to manipulate gut chemistry through diet, probiotics, or other therapies will need to account for both microbial activity and the body's own metabolic capabilities.

Much of the experimental evidence comes from animals and laboratory studies, so additional research will be needed to determine how these mechanisms influence long-term health outcomes in people.

Nevertheless, a better understanding of the relationship between different food components and microbial metabolism could eventually make dietary advice more precise and help researchers identify new therapeutic strategies.

"Beyond that," said Rabinowitz, "a clearer picture of how different foods interact with the microbiome to modulate the production of bacterial metabolites will help sharpen the guidance nutritionists and doctors can give to people for disease prevention and therapy."

These studies were funded by the Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research, the National Institutes of Health, the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, the Princeton Alliance for Collaborative Research and Innovation, Princeton University.

Aside from his post as Director of the Princeton Branch of the Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research, Joshua Rabinowitz is Professor in the Department of Chemistry & Lewis-Sigler Institute for Integrative Genomics and a member of the Rutgers Cancer Institute.
